title: Tight Lower Bounds for ℓ 2 Sampling

statements.text: An (𝜖, 𝛿)-ℓ2 -sampler with frequency estimation requires a sketching dimension of at least 1 Ω(log2 𝑛 + 2 log 𝑛). 𝜖 Moreover, storing such a sketch for vectors with poly(𝑛) sized entries requires 1 Ω(log3 𝑛 + 2 log2 𝑛) 𝜖 bits of space. 1.2 Preliminaries ℓ2 samplers. We use the following definition for an ℓ2 sampling sketch. For us, we only consider sketches with constant failure probability. Additionally, while ℓ2 samplers exist, our lower bounds hold against samplers that perform ℓ2 sampling up to constants. So we use this less restrictive definition here.

An ℓ2 sampling sketch is an algorithm that observes a linear sketch 𝑆𝑣 of 𝑣 ∈ R𝑛 with 𝑆 : R𝑛 → R𝑚 , and chooses to either output FAIL, with probability at most 12 , or output a coordinate ℓ. Conditioned on not outputting FAIL, the outputted coordinate must satisfy Pr(ℓ = 𝑖) = (1 ± 12 )𝑣𝑖2 . ∥𝑣 ∥ 2 Existing ℓ2 sampling sketches are also able to output accurate frequency estimates for the sampled coordinate. We will provide a lower bound against such sketches as well.

From the lemma above, we may assume that the entries of 𝐴 are integers bounded by 𝑛 in magnitude. Note that this is just a rescaled and discretized version of Problem 2.1. Also let D1 be the continuous version of this distribution: N (0, 𝑛 2𝑐 𝐼𝑛 ) + 𝑛𝑐 ⌊2𝑟 /2 ⌋𝑒𝑘 where 𝑟 and 𝑘 are as above. Also let D𝑖,𝑟,𝑘 denote the distribution D𝑖 conditioned on the values of 𝑟 and 𝑘. Let 𝑔 be the (deterministic) recovery function such that 𝑔(𝐴𝑣) is the output of the ℓ2 sampler on the input vector 𝑣. By Lemma 6, we may assume without loss of generality that condition 1 of Theorem 4.1 holds, and we may ensure that condition 2 holds by choosing the constant 𝑐 appropriately. Now, let 𝐴D𝑖 be the distribution gotten by applying 𝐴 to a sample from D𝑖 , and let round(·) be the function that rounds to the nearest lattice point of the lattice defined by 𝐴. By Theorem 4.1, we have that TVD(round(𝐴D1,𝑟,𝑘 ), 𝐴D0,𝑟,𝑘 ) ≤ 𝑛 −𝐶 , and therefore TVD(𝑔(round(𝐴D1,𝑟,𝑘 )), 𝑔(𝐴D0,𝑟,𝑘 )) ≤ 𝑛 −𝐶 , for all 𝑟, 𝑘. Since the payout is bounded by 𝑛, this means that for any 𝑟, 𝑘 the expected payout differs by at most 1/poly(𝑛) between the two distributions. So if there is an algorithm to obtain expected payout Ω(1) on the second distribution, then it must be possible to obtain Ω(1) expected payout on the first distribution. So by our lower bound Theorem 2.1, 𝐴 must have Ω(log2 𝑛) rows, and so storing the sketch 𝐴𝑣 requires Ω(log3 𝑛) bits. □
